newsitem.title: USA: What will the Fed do? Don't expect answer in polls.
newsitem.headline: What will the Fed do? Don't expect answer in polls.

text.p: If the U.S. Treasury market seems to be confused over what the Federal Reserve will or won't do at Tuesday's policy-setting meeting, there's a simple reason: It is.
There's certainly no shortage of opinion and as usual, news organisations have been busy gathering it and sharing it with their readers.
More than a dozen surveys of financial experts have been produced by the various news agencies that serve financial subscribers.
That thorough examination of opinion has revealed that just about half of the experts expect the Fed to raise rates and about half don't.

For instance, polls of the 39 primary dealers, the companies that buy and sell government debt to public investors -- and presumably are tuned in to the Fed's mood -- found that about half expect the Fed to raise interest rates.

Only one, a survey of 16 Wall Street analysts conducted by MCM MoneyWatch Inc., a New York consultant group, was decisive. In that survey, 12 of the analysts -- 75 percent -- said they expected a rate hike.
Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp., suggested there were too many surveys out there. So many reporters call him for his opinion, that he's taken a new approach.
"I started polling the reporters for their call on what the Fed would do."
And just in case the "man on the street" can shed any light on the situation, MSNBC is polling Internet users.
The result? More of the same. Of more than 2,500 people who responded, 52 percent expect the Fed to raise rates.
